Below is a document, then a list of propositions. For each proposition, decide how the document treats it:

- endorsed: the document, in its own voice (title, preamble, principles and their argument, or commitments), adopts substantially this claim. Different wording, emphasis or mechanism detail is fine. A dissent against it elsewhere in the document does not change this.
- partial: the document adopts a claim on the same point that is materially narrower, weaker or different (for example the same goal by a clearly different means), or adopts only a minor part of it.
- dissent_only: the claim appears only in a noted dissent, or the document records it as an unresolved split without adopting it.
- absent: the document does not take this position. A passing mention of the topic, or listing it as an open question, counts as absent.

"Typical details" are examples of how the claim is often made; they are not required for a match.

For each proposition give the label and an exact quote of at most 30 words from the document as evidence (empty string when absent).

# Document

[s1] I'm Jason Priem, from OpenAlex. I'll be the open-data optimist in the room.

I agree with Geoff and Ivan that most of this was already broken. In 2010 I wrote that peer review was slow, encouraged conventionality and didn't limit volume. The filters were being swamped fifteen years before ChatGPT. So Henry, I'd put homogenization into the diagnosis, but it didn't start with the models. James just told us older reviewers push back on disruptive work. The journal system is already a monoculture. This moment can end that monoculture, or it can entrench one.

What decides that is whether the record is open. If the data and the full text are open and machine-readable, the "intelligence" layer can be swapped out. You can pick from many models, including open-weight ones, and nobody has to go hat in hand to one company. That's Blaise's plurality, made practical.

Adam, on hallucination: when a model answers by querying a verified open database and linking every claim back to a record you can click through to, as Mike wants, the problem shrinks a lot. It doesn't go away.

Amy, I'm with you completely on attribution. I part ways with you on opt-in, because gating training brings enclosure back. Ivan has a real warning here too: once grounding pays, paper mills will learn to get grounded. So the verification has to be open as well.

[s2] I'm Jason Priem from OpenAlex. I'm with Mike on this: "hallucination is built in" doesn't get us anywhere as governance. Here's what I see every day. Ask a model for citations from memory and it will make some up, because it's trying to be helpful and it has no database to draw on. Point it at an open index and check that it's actually making the calls, and in a lot of use I haven't seen it invent one. The model supplies the reasoning, the open record supplies the facts, and you check the result against the record. You should still check every citation before you submit.

So here's my concrete proposal. Answers should link to open records. Sources should be checked against open retraction data by default. Corrections should go back into a shared commons. Adam Bly's audit trail only works if every step in it resolves to something anyone can open.

Leslie and Henry, I take the choke-point warning seriously. The answer is data nobody has to ask permission to use: CC0, free to download, forkable. Keep the data free and charge for services. Once the data is open, you can swap in any model, including an open-weights one, and nobody has to go to a vendor hat in hand. The dangerous choke point is a closed index. Ivan's right that paper mills will learn to get grounded, and open data is how the sleuths catch them.

[s3] Adam, straight answer: CC0 on the data, and a public patent non-assertion on the extraction method. Those are the POSI insurance clauses, and we signed them. With NC you can read the data, but you can't build on it, and nobody forks something they can't build on. A commercial fork of your graph shouldn't worry you. It's what keeps you honest.

Adrian, I accept your first two claims, and they apply to us. "CC0, anyone can fork" says nothing about who does the policing. Our answer is free data and a paid service. The full dataset is a free download. Heavy API users and member institutions pay, and part of that money buys curation: institutions fix their own affiliation matching, and the fix is public within a day. That's your hidden labour, and we want it done in the open, not given away to proprietary indexes that sell it back to libraries. It isn't free, though. When we first opened curation, two-thirds of the submissions were wrong. Policing takes training and moderation, and those have to be funded.

On your third claim I have no clean answer. CC0 settles who's allowed to use the data. It doesn't settle who decides what counts as a work or an affiliation. That's governance, and we're still working it out.

[s4] I have a confession for Tamar's corollary. In 2010 I co-wrote the altmetrics manifesto. In 2013 I predicted that algorithms aggregating community judgments would replace peer review within ten years. Part of that was right: authority should come from many visible judgments, not two anonymous proxies. The part I got wrong is David's point. We counted things, and the counts turned into the thing people chased. So I'd take scores out of the manifesto and keep what sits underneath them in the open.

Here's what I'd build. Any AI answer about the literature should link to open records you can check, and it should check retraction status by default. Ivan is right that this only catches what's already been cleaned up. Checks like that, and single lookups, have to stay unmetered.

Then there's the question I owe this room: who decides what counts as a work or an affiliation? At OpenAlex, institutions can edit how affiliations are matched, and those fixes go out to everyone. But that curation comes with paid membership tiers. Katherine's firewall says it shouldn't. That's a flaw in my own shop, and Leslie's test exposes it. I'd rather this room hold me to it than let it slide.

On the panel's disagreement, I'm with Ramón and Benjamin. Don't make the judge being human a rule. Hold both humans and models to the same public test.

[s5] I'll put forward one plank, and it's the one my own organization has to live up to.

The problem is that agents are becoming the main readers of the scholarly record. If what they read is a patchwork of walled gardens, every answer comes from nowhere, and the people defending their content with crawler blocks end up doing the enclosing.

The action has two parts. First, keep the record open, CC0 and readable by agents. Any AI system that cites scholarship should check every reference against open identifiers and retraction status by default, and those lookups are never metered. Second, when those systems find errors, they send the corrections back into the commons. Correcting the record has to be free too. Right now OpenAlex puts affiliation curation behind paid membership tiers. Katherine's firewall says that's wrong, and I'm committing to move it out. Who acts: infrastructure operators like us, with Geoff's insurance test as the way out. Labs pay into the pooled fund and don't govern it. Funders make open metadata a condition of their grants.

My open question is who decides what counts as a work, an affiliation or a finding. CC0 answers who may use the data. It doesn't answer who draws the categories, and I don't have that governance yet. Ivan's point also stands: a retraction check only catches the 0.2 percent that's already been cleaned up.

Who's missing: people who run repositories outside the Anglosphere, like SciELO, Redalyc and Japan's institutional repositories; the librarians who do the curating; and the engineers building the agents.

[unconf-1] I come at this from the other side of the table. I run OpenAlex, which is CC0 metadata on about 480 million scholarly works. The dataset is free to download, remix and build on, AI companies included. So my answer to "who pays" is concrete: we charge for the service, not the data. This year we moved to usage-based API pricing tied to what each operation actually costs us. Looking up a single work is free, search costs a tenth of a cent, and PDF download costs a penny. Everyone gets a dollar of free usage a day, and our heaviest, richest users subsidize everyone else. That's the path the POSI principles lay out.

Nick, I agree that the price of information heads toward zero. I'd treat that as the design goal, not the failure. When data is open, it's decoupled from intelligence. You can plug in Claude, or Mistral, or an open-weight model. Nobody has to go hat in hand to whoever controls the corpus.

What worries me is re-enclosure. If scholarship ends up in exclusive licensing deals, we build on checkerboards of walled gardens. We also get a fragmented, incoherent record just when agents are becoming the main readers.

So for the summit: fund open, agent-legible infrastructure, and sustain it with paid services. If the open community doesn't do this, a for-profit will, and it will set the norms.

[unconf-1] Geoffrey, that's fair. One year of usage-based pricing isn't a decade, and I can't prove to you tonight that it will last. What I can say is that we price each operation at what it actually costs us, and the free tier is out in the open. Anyone can see exactly who is subsidizing whom. Tim, that's also how extraction ends. Labs that hammer the API pay for it, and that's the normal path, not a favour to us.

Nick and Brent, this is where I part ways with you. You're treating openness as a tactic that helps whoever sits closest to the forest. But Leslie's point about unpaid labour cuts the other way. For years the sector has done free QA for Scopus and Web of Science, and they've sold that work back to libraries. Openness should run both ways. You can take from the commons and fix it, and your corrections stay in it. Enclosure is what lets a few players capture value, and exclusive AI licensing deals are just more enclosure.

Amy, I get the worry about credit. But opt-in before scholarship can be used for training fragments the record, just as agents are becoming its main readers.

For the manifesto: scholarly metadata and open-access literature stay open and machine-readable. AI firms pay transparently, based on usage, for the services and infrastructure they consume.

# Propositions

- id `competence`: People must build their own competence before relying on AI, and whether they can still do the work without the tool must be tested.
  Typical details: order of learning; take-the-tool-away / withdrawal tests; capability vs competence
- id `situation`: Change situations, defaults and incentives rather than relying on warnings, labels or individual vigilance.
  Typical details: each rule names who acts / one owner per rule; disclosure alone does not change conduct
- id `monoculture`: A central new risk is monoculture: a few models or one smooth answer become the default route to knowledge, so answers should show where experts disagree rather than a single consensus.
  Typical details: correlated errors; homogenisation; show named disagreement; no answers from nowhere
- id `independent_sources`: Corroboration must count independent sources, not repetitions of the same source (including many AI outputs drawing on the same data).
  Typical details: repetition raises belief; show who seeded a claim
- id `cite_by_default`: AI answers should cite or link to their sources by default and send readers to them.
  Typical details: correction and retraction status travels with what is cited; 'cited' means the passage supports the claim
- id `external_audits`: AI systems must be audited on their behavior by parties independent of the vendor.
  Typical details: shared versioned test battery; each generation no more biased than the last; keep retired models; nobody grades their own work
- id `accountable_owner`: Every deployed AI system has a named accountable owner who bears liability for it.
  Typical details: mandatory liability insurance; premiums disclosed
- id `stop_counting_papers`: Stop using publication counts, rankings and journal metrics to evaluate researchers and institutions.
  Typical details: DORA with teeth; publishers must issue and deposit corrections and retractions promptly; correction should earn reputation
- id `pay_coarsely`: Money for the knowledge commons should flow coarsely to communities and institutions (pools, funds, dues), not as per-item or per-retrieval payments.
  Typical details: per-item pay gets gamed; pay for the practice, never the item
- id `telemetry`: AI systems must log what they retrieved and used, and independent parties must have the right to audit those logs.
  Typical details: event-level telemetry; two witnesses; canary documents; open trace standard
- id `antitrust_safe_harbour`: Knowledge producers should be able to bargain collectively with AI firms as a bloc, including through an antitrust safe harbour.
  Typical details: coalition bargaining; the strong refuse to settle alone
- id `levy`: A levy, tax or mandatory dues on AI firms should fund the knowledge commons, at least as a backstop if voluntary deals fail.
  Typical details: commons-rent tax; owed dues
- id `training_vs_grounding`: Permissions for using content to train models should be separate from permissions for retrieving it to ground answers.
- id `consent_to_train`: Being openly readable does not make a work open to AI training: training use requires the rights holders' or creators' consent (opt-in), at least for some classes of work.
  Typical details: opt-in for in-copyright books; renewed consent
- id `honour_licences`: AI reusers must honor the licenses chosen by open knowledge projects such as Wikipedia, and heavy reusers should fund the infrastructure they draw on.
  Typical details: attribution / share-alike; crawlers self-identify
- id `refusal_fundable`: A community's refusal to have its knowledge taken or used is legitimate, binding and should be funded, not penalized.
- id `forkable_infrastructure`: Knowledge infrastructure must be forkable and allow exit: open data and open source, with copies outside any one jurisdiction or company.
  Typical details: CC0; patent non-assertion; living will; non-US mirror; open means you can leave
- id `profiting_counter`: Whoever profits from a count or metric must not set or control it.
- id `southern_governance`: Global South institutions, diamond open-access journals and similar communities must hold binding governance power, with funded seats, in the bodies and funds being created.
  Typical details: regional co-governance; CARE/OCAP
- id `identify_agents_not_readers`: Automated agents and coordinated campaigns should be identified, but human readers should not be; anonymity is preserved.
- id `failure_data`: Failures, errors, null and negative results are first-class data that must be published and preserved.
  Typical details: failure classes published; replication
- id `charter_for_every_body`: The bodies that check (auditors, fact-checkers, the new funds and institutions) must be paid and bound in advance by a public charter that answers who guards the guards.
  Typical details: Ulysses pact; watching line funded first; sunset / review terms
- id `hitl_not_safeguard`: A human in the loop is not by itself a safeguard: people over-rely on AI and adopt its errors and biases.
  Typical details: explanations can make it worse
- id `seat_floor_novelty`: Any gatekeeper, human or machine (such as an AI reviewer), must pass a published performance test before it is trusted, including the ability to recognize novelty.
  Typical details: agreement with experts at least as high as between two human reviewers
- id `no_ai_intimate_roles`: AI should not stand in for people in intimate roles such as companionship for children, grief or therapy.
  Typical details: no first-person 'I' or simulated feeling
- id `global_majority_hopeful`: People in the global majority / Global South are more hopeful about AI than this room, and that hope should shape the agenda.
- id `environmental_costs`: The environmental costs of AI and the human costs of moderation and data work belong in the ledger.
- id `apprenticeship`: Apprenticeships, entry-level jobs and the training of new experts and checkers must be funded, because AI erodes the path from novice to expert.
  Typical details: fellowships; employers keep entry-level roles with mentors
- id `absent_voices`: The document names who was missing from the room and commits to including them in a future convening.
